q: At point A in the money market, what is the equilibrium nominal interest rate?
options: 6 percent
4 percent
8 percent
12 percent
feedback: Point A is where MD0 intersects MS0, at a nominal interest rate of 6 percent.

q: The money-supply curve moves from MS0 at 100 to MS1 at 125. What happens to the equilibrium nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
It stays at 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
feedback: With money demand fixed, the larger money supply moves equilibrium down MD0 from 4 percent to 2 percent.

q: When the money-supply line moves left from 100 to 75, how does the equilibrium interest rate respond?
options: It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
It stays at 4 percent
It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
feedback: With money demand fixed, the smaller money supply moves equilibrium up MD0 from 4 percent to 6 percent.

q: Which labeled point is the original equilibrium where MD0 intersects MS0?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
Point D
feedback: The original curves MD0 and MS0 intersect at point B, quantity 75 and interest rate 3.

q: In the left panel, money demand rises from MD0 to MD1 while MS0 stays fixed. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2 percent
It stays at 2 percent
It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
feedback: With fixed money supply, the higher money-demand curve raises the equilibrium interest rate from point A to point B.

q: A student says a fall in the interest rate from 8 percent to 6 percent would shift MD0 to the right. What is the best correction?
options: Interest-rate changes move along MD0; they do not shift MD0.
Interest-rate changes shift MD0 because the rate is on the axis.
Interest-rate changes shift MS0 while MD0 stays fixed.
Interest-rate changes shift both MD0 and MS0 together.
feedback: The interest rate is the price variable on the money-demand curve. Changing it moves the economy along MD0.

q: A student says the fall in the interest rate from 4 percent to 2 percent proves money demand shifted left. What does the graph actually show?
options: MD0 shifts left while money supply remains fixed at MS0 throughout.
MD0 and money supply both shift right to separate new curves.
MD0 is fixed; MS shifts right and equilibrium moves along MD0.
Neither money demand nor money supply changes in the diagram.
feedback: MD0 is unchanged. The new equilibrium is reached by moving along the same money-demand curve after MS shifts right.

q: A student says the rise in the interest rate from 4 percent to 6 percent proves money demand shifted right. What does the graph actually show?
options: MD0 is fixed; MS shifts left and equilibrium moves along MD0.
MD0 shifts right while money supply remains fixed at MS0 throughout.
MD0 and money supply both shift left to separate new curves.
Neither money demand nor money supply changes in the diagram.
feedback: MD0 is unchanged. The higher interest rate comes from the smaller money supply, causing a movement along MD0.

q: Compare original point B with simultaneous-shift point C. What happens to quantity of money and the nominal interest rate?
options: Quantity rises from 75 to 100 while the interest rate falls from 3 percent to 1 percent
Quantity stays at 75 while the interest rate rises from 3 percent to 6 percent
Quantity rises from 75 to 100 while the interest rate rises from 3 percent to 4 percent
Quantity falls from 100 to 75 while the interest rate falls from 4 percent to 3 percent
feedback: The increase in money supply raises equilibrium quantity, while the simultaneous increase in money demand is strong enough to leave the interest rate one point higher than at B.

q: A student says the money-demand increase should shift aggregate demand right because people want to hold more money. What is the strongest correction using the graph?
options: With MS fixed, higher MD raises rates; spending falls and AD shifts left.
With MS fixed, higher MD lowers rates; spending rises and AD shifts right.
Higher MD creates extra money automatically, so interest rates fall.
Money demand and aggregate demand are the same curve and shift together.
feedback: Money demand is demand for liquid balances, not aggregate expenditure. With fixed supply, more money demand raises the interest rate and can reduce spending.

q: Moving downward along MD0 from a higher to a lower interest rate, what happens to the quantity of money demanded?
options: The quantity of money demanded falls.
The quantity of money supplied rises.
The money-demand curve shifts left.
The quantity of money demanded rises.
feedback: Holding other determinants fixed, lower interest rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding money, so quantity of money demanded rises.

q: What is the change in the equilibrium nominal interest rate when money supply rises from 100 to 125?
options: An increase of 2 percentage points
A decrease of 2 percentage points
A decrease of 25 percentage points
No change
feedback: The equilibrium interest rate falls from 4 percent to 2 percent, a 2-percentage-point decrease.

q: What is the change in the equilibrium nominal interest rate when money supply falls from 100 to 75?
options: A decrease of 2 percentage points
An increase of 25 percentage points
No change
An increase of 2 percentage points
feedback: The equilibrium interest rate rises from 4 percent to 6 percent, a 2-percentage-point increase.

q: If money demand increases from MD0 to MD1 at the same time money supply increases from MS0 to MS1, which point is the resulting equilibrium?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
Point D
feedback: The simultaneous shifts produce the intersection of MD1 and MS1, point C.

q: By how much does real GDP change from point A to point B in the right panel?
feedback: Read real GDP at A and B in the right panel: 150 − 105 = 45.

q: If the nominal interest rate were temporarily above point A while MS0 stayed fixed, what adjustment pressure would the graph imply?
options: Excess money demand pushes the rate farther above A.
Excess money supply pushes the rate down toward A.
Money supply shifts right until the rate rises above A.
Money demand shifts left until the rate remains above A.
feedback: Above equilibrium, the quantity of money demanded is less than the fixed money supply. Portfolio adjustment pushes the interest rate back down toward equilibrium.

q: Starting from the money-market change shown, which downstream effect would normally follow?
options: Lower rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Higher rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
Higher rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
feedback: The standard transmission channel runs from more money to lower interest rates to more interest-sensitive spending and higher aggregate demand.

q: After the money-supply change from MS0 to MS1 shown in the graph, which spending-and-AD response should follow?
options: Higher rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
Higher rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
feedback: The standard contractionary chain runs from less money to higher interest rates to less interest-sensitive spending and lower aggregate demand.

q: Money demand rises from MD0 to MD1. Which central-bank response shown partially offsets the interest-rate increase without restoring the original 3-percent rate?
options: Lower MS from MS1 to MS0; C→A lowers the rate.
Keep MS at MS0; B→D lowers the rate.
Shift MD back to MD0; A→C raises the rate.
Raise MS from MS0 to MS1; A→C lowers the rate.
feedback: The demand increase alone raises the rate from B to A. Expanding money supply then lowers it from 6 to 4 percent at C, partially but not fully offsetting the increase.

q: Which complete chain is consistent with the two-panel graph?
options: MD ↑; rate ↓; interest-sensitive spending ↑; AD →; GDP and prices ↑.
MD ↑; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↓; AD ←; GDP and prices ↓.
MS ↑; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↓; AD ←; GDP and prices ↑.
MD ↓; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↑; AD →; GDP and prices ↑.
feedback: The panels show the full liquidity-preference transmission from a money-demand increase to a higher rate and lower aggregate demand.

q: At point A, what quantity of money clears the market?
feedback: The vertical money-supply curve MS0 is fixed at quantity 100, and MD0 intersects it at point A.

q: Which feature of MS0 shows that this model treats the nominal money supply as fixed?
options: MD0 is downward sloping as the interest rate changes.
Point A lies where the two curves cross in equilibrium.
MS0 is vertical at a fixed money quantity.
The interest rate is measured on the vertical axis.
feedback: In the standard liquidity-preference model, the central bank fixes the nominal quantity of money, so MS is vertical.

q: How much farther right is MS1 than MS0 in the graph?
feedback: Money supply increases from 100 to 125, a rise of 25 units.

q: Which central-bank action is most consistent with the shift from MS0 to MS1?
options: An expansionary action that increases the money supply
A contractionary action that decreases the money supply
A rise in real income that shifts money demand right
A higher price level that shifts money demand right
feedback: The graph shows a rightward shift of the vertical money-supply curve, which is expansionary.

q: Measure the leftward distance from MS0 to MS1. How much smaller is the money supply?
feedback: Money supply falls from 100 to 75, a decrease of 25 units.

q: Which contractionary central-bank action could produce the displayed money-supply shift?
options: An expansionary action that increases the money supply
A rise in real income that increases money demand
A contractionary action that reduces the money supply
A lower price level that reduces money demand
feedback: The graph shows a leftward shift of the vertical money-supply curve, which is contractionary.

q: If only money demand increases from MD0 to MD1 while MS0 stays fixed, which point becomes the new equilibrium?
options: Point B
Point C
Point D
Point A
feedback: Holding MS0 at 75, the higher MD1 curve intersects it at point A, interest rate 6.

q: With MD0 unchanged, locate the equilibrium created solely by the increase in money supply. Which point is it?
options: Point D
Point A
Point B
Point C
feedback: Holding MD0 fixed, the larger MS1 intersects it at point D, quantity 100 and interest rate 1.

q: Which change in the right panel accompanies the higher interest rate shown in the money market?
options: Aggregate demand shifts right from AD1 to AD0
Aggregate demand shifts left from AD0 to AD1
SRAS shifts left while aggregate demand stays fixed
LRAS shifts right
feedback: The graph links the higher interest rate to lower interest-sensitive spending and a leftward shift of aggregate demand.

q: Which mechanism best connects the change from A to B in the left panel with the change from A to B in the right panel?
options: Higher rates directly increase the money supply.
Higher rates increase potential output and LRAS.
Higher rates reduce interest-sensitive spending.
Higher rates lower all production costs and SRAS.
feedback: The standard link is through interest-sensitive components of spending, especially investment.

q: The left panel shows money supply increasing from MS0 to MS1. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
It stays at 6 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 2 percent
feedback: The increase in money supply moves the money-market equilibrium from A at 6 percent to B at 4 percent.

q: In the contractionary two-panel diagram, what happens to the nominal interest rate after the money-supply change?
options: It rises from 2.75 percent to 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2.75 percent
It stays at 2.75 percent
It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
feedback: The smaller money supply moves equilibrium from A at 2.75 percent to B at 4 percent.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes what changes in the two panels?
options: MD shifts right and MS is traversed; SRAS shifts right along fixed AD.
MS shifts left and MD is traversed; AD shifts left along fixed SRAS.
MS shifts right and MD is traversed; AD shifts right along fixed SRAS.
Both panels show movements along fixed demand and supply curves.
feedback: Different markets are being linked. Money supply shifts first; the resulting rate change affects spending and shifts AD.

q: A student says AD1 is lower because the central bank directly reduced real GDP. What is the better interpretation?
options: Lower MS raises rates; lower interest-sensitive spending shifts AD left.
Lower MS lowers rates; higher interest-sensitive spending shifts AD right.
The central bank directly sets real GDP and moves AD to that quantity.
A rightward MD shift raises rates and directly shifts SRAS to the left.
feedback: Monetary policy works through a transmission mechanism. The central bank acts on money/financial conditions, which influence spending and AD.

q: Which sequence matches the changes from point A to point B across the two panels?
options: MS ↑ → rate ↑ → spending ↓ → AD ← → output and price level ↓
MS ↑ → rate ↓ → spending ↑ → AD → → output and price level ↑
MS ↓ → rate ↓ → spending ↑ → AD → → output and price level ↑
MD ↑ → rate ↓ → spending ↑ → SRAS → → output and price level ↓
feedback: That is the standard expansionary monetary-policy transmission chain represented by the two panels.

q: Which causal chain matches the changes from A to B in the second two-panel diagram?
options: MS ↓ → rate ↓ → spending ↑ → AD → → output and price level ↑
MS ↑ → rate ↑ → spending ↓ → AD ← → output and price level ↓
MD ↓ → rate ↑ → spending ↓ → SRAS ← → output and price level ↑
MS ↓ → rate ↑ → spending ↓ → AD ← → output and price level ↓
feedback: That is the standard contractionary monetary-policy transmission chain shown across the two panels.

q: What conclusion is supported by the change from A to B across the two panels?
options: The illustrated easing raises rates and lowers both GDP and the price level.
The illustrated easing raises potential GDP by shifting LRAS to the right.
The illustrated easing raises GDP while leaving the price level unchanged.
The illustrated easing lowers rates and raises both GDP and the price level.
feedback: The graph supports the specific illustrated changes. It does not establish a universal fixed coefficient between interest rates and GDP.

q: What macroeconomic conclusion is supported by the contractionary A-to-B movement across both panels?
options: The illustrated tightening lowers rates and raises both GDP and the price level.
The illustrated tightening raises rates and lowers both GDP and the price level.
The illustrated tightening lowers potential GDP by shifting LRAS to the left.
The illustrated tightening lowers GDP while raising the price level.
feedback: The graph supports the specific policy chain and depicted outcomes, not a universal mechanical coefficient.

q: Which aggregate-demand change accompanies the lower interest rate in the right panel?
options: AD shifts left from AD1 to AD0
SRAS shifts right while AD stays fixed
LRAS shifts left
AD shifts right from AD0 to AD1
feedback: The lower interest rate stimulates interest-sensitive spending, shifting aggregate demand right.

q: In the expansionary two-panel diagram, how many units does real GDP rise from A to B?
feedback: Read real GDP at A and B: 125 − 100 = 25 units.

q: In the right panel, which aggregate-demand change accompanies the higher interest rate generated on the left?
options: AD shifts right from AD1 to AD0
AD shifts left from AD0 to AD1
SRAS shifts left while AD stays fixed
LRAS shifts right
feedback: The higher interest rate reduces interest-sensitive spending, shifting aggregate demand left.

q: In the contractionary two-panel diagram, how many units does real GDP fall from A to B?
feedback: Read real GDP at A and B: 125 − 100 = 25 units.
